speechtext:

In view of the increasing tension, as evidenced by the demonstration on Parliament Hill today, in the long drawn-out contract negotiations between the government of Canada and the Canadian Union of
Postal Workers which threatens further work stoppages in the Post Office, and the growing demand for action by members of parliament from both sides of the House, including government members, as evidenced by a question directed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) on February 23, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That the government set up immediately a special committee of parliament to investigate the Post Office to bring in recommendations for solutions and, in particular, to consider the advisability of converting Canada Post to a Crown corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent necessity and national significance. The Ottawa Journal of March 2 quotes Mr. Al Johnson, president of Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as having said before the Task Force on Canadian Unity: "I believe the Canadian people are not searching for absolute truth in the news media". That would be a futile search. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin):
That this House, through Mr. Speaker, inform the president of the CBC that the people of Canada are intelligent and sophisticated enough to make their own decisions if the CBC and other news media provide them with the facts, and that he show more respect for the intelligence and judgment of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, the minister issued a press release announcing the intention of the government of Canada to go to the United States on a

borrowing venture. What is surprising about that is the amount of money the government proposes to borrow.
As the minister must surely know, if we wanted to maintain our traditional reserves in United States dollars, we would need to borrow almost $5 billion U.S. Can the minister tell the House why he is seeking to borrow only the token amount of $750 million, in light of what has happened to the Canadian dollar?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we decided that was the appropriate amount of money to borrow, in the circumstances.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. My question was why this amount was decided upon. There is a very real question about whether the decisions that this minister calls appropriate are appropriate in fact. 1 should like to ask the minister whether he considered indulging in the normal practice of trying to place this proposed issue privately, and whether he was turned down. I should also like the minister to tell the House whether the original request was for a larger amount than $750 million.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we had both options, and we decided to go public. The amount was the amount discussed between my agent, the governor of the Bank of Canada, and the institutions. It is a public issue. More details will be made public later on.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Once again, the minister did not answer the question, Mr. Speaker. He said they had both options. My question was whether they decided to go public because they were turned down privately. I hope the minister can address himself to that question. Since he has made this decision to go to the Securities and Exchange Commission of the United States, he must surely know it will be necessary for the government of Canada to file a registration statement with the SEC. This will mean the Minister of Finance is proposing to give the Securities and Exchange Commission of another country more information about our economic situation than he is giving the House of Commons of Canada.
Will the minister give us a commitment now that he will file on the floor of the House of Commons and make available to the people of Canada exactly the same information he is going to make available to an agency of another government, before he makes that public declaration to the SEC?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 knew I had to file a prospectus like any other institution that goes to the American market. I was aware of it and I have no problem with it at all. 1 think the story we can tell about Canada is a very good one. When I said I had the two options, I hoped the hon. member would have realized that when you have an option you can choose either way. We decided to go public. We were not turned down on a private placement, but we felt it was better in the present situation to go public.
March 3, 1978

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Minister of Finance tell us what reasoning led the government of Canada to take the quite unusual step of going public in this matter, rather than making a private borrowing? It may be unprecedented-I have not had a chance to check the record-but why did the government of Canada choose that option, rather than the more normal option?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING TO BOLSTER VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have chosen that avenue because we thought is was the best at the moment. If we make a private investment, our options are more limited. We wanted to have different blocks of bonds over various periods of time and we thought it would be easier to operate this way because the investments will thus be more diversified than if they were invested in one or two American institutions.
I also would like to add, with leave of the House, that the interest rates are generally better when one goes public.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Bearing in mind that we have lost about $750 million in United States reserves since the end of January, and the minister has indicated he is only proposing to borrow $750 million in the United States market, would the minister indicate if they intend to borrow still more in some future month?
Mr. Speaker, when we decide to borrow more, if we decide to borrow more, I will be glad to advise the public and the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Bearing in mind that it is widely speculated that the dollar may go still lower, with the faint effort put forth by the government in raising foreign funds, bearing in mind that the inflationary impact of the falling dollar is much more severe in Canada than it is in the United States, and bearing in mind that our dollar has fallen 31 per cent in relation to the Japanese yen since October 20, 1976, and 28 per cent in terms of the West German deut-schemark, for example, would the minister indicate if he still believes that he will achieve a 6 per cent inflation rate in the current year, bearing in mind the heavy inflationary impact his falling dollar is going to have on Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I think there is some problem, when the Canadian dollar loses some value, in terms of imports. Imports are increasing, costs are increasing, and it could put some pressure on inflation; I recognize that. But I am not advised to change the forecast for the end of the year. At the same time, I would like to report to the hon. member that 1 receive telephone calls and telegrams every day from many manufacturers in Ontario who tell me that they like the dollar the way it is at present, because the export position of Canada is improving considerably.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Bearing in mind the consequences of our falling dollar, and bearing in mind that any foreign funds the minister may borrow is simply stalling the inevitable, would the minister indicate what concrete proposals he intends to put before this House to reduce the balance of payment deficit which this country is incurring? By the end of the year it will be $20 billion that we have lost in foreign exchange. What does the minister propose to do to end this steady outflow of our funds?
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, we have a floating dollar at present and the level of the dollar is determined by the market. Our interventions in February were made to ensure an orderly floating of the dollar, since it is the responsibility of the Governor of the Bank Canada to do so, and the value of the dollar is fluctuating. We do not know exactly at what level the dollar should be. The market will determine that. The hon. member is always giving the impression that we have huge losses when we are losing American dollars in our reserves but at the same time, we are improving our own liquid assets as it is possible that we will be borrowing less on the Canadian market if we borrow on the American market. I wish the hon. member would not give the impression that we are losing $700 million, because such is not the case. We have exchanged American dollars for Canadian dollars.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Considering that the steady decline in the value of the Canadian dollar is due to circumstances here, as it is due to circumstances in other countries that are badly managed, namely, an economy that is persistently bad in terms of the rate of inflation and one that has more than one million unemployed, can the minister tell us why he took the $750 million, costly step that he has taken, instead of bringing forward measures that would lead to higher levels of investment and more job creation in the Canadian economy? Surely that is what the Canadian economy is looking for.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. speechtext: The hon. gentleman should realize that before we bring in a budget we should wait to see the effect of the measures which were taken only two months ago. If the hon. member is advocating that we should stimulate it still further, he should not encourage his colleagues to get up in the House and complain that we are running too big a deficit. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in this debate on Bill C-17 to comment briefly on some of the concerns 1 have about this CNR refinancing bill, in the context of our national rail transportation policy in general and the problems we encounter in many areas of Canada because we do not have a national transportation policy due to the lack of initiative of the Liberal government under the current Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, over the past decade, I am afraid, has allowed the situation to go from bad to worse.
This bill is an attempt to recapitalize $808 million of the CNR debt which stands at approximately $2 billion. We support the concept of trying to reduce the debt of the CNR. We think it has to be brought on to a more equal footing with the CPR, and therefore we say this recapitalization is long overdue. As a Crown corporation the CNR has carried this burden for a number of years while competing on an unfair basis with the CPR.
It should not be forgotten that the CNR was formed when private railway companies went bankrupt. In 1919 the government of the day acknowledged that rail service was an essential service and that railways should not be allowed to fold up and leave communities stranded. The history of transportation and of other areas of endeavour in this country shows that the government stepped in to maintain an essential service and, in doing so, of course saddled itself with a huge debt and committed itself to paying off the private owners and shareholders in the company. As a result the CNR has been burdened with that debt over the years.
We should not forget that the government has helped the private railway company as well. I am sometimes amused at the distortion of history that we see in the advertising of private groups in this country. 1 think of the Insurance Bureau of Canada and, to some extent, of the CPR. They like to glorify private enterprise and imply that it developed this country all on its own. Anyone who reads Canadian economic history realizes, of course, that is only half the truth. There is a long tradition of government involvement in Canada through direct subsidy, taxation measures, and Crown corporations, which did what private capital and industry was unable or unwilling to do. We should remind ourselves that at the close of the 19th century the CPR received $25 billion in outright grants from the federal government and a grant of 25 million acres of land, a very handsome subsidy in those days.
When we talk of private and public transportation we should not forget the context in which both were developed. It was considered that transportation was a service very important to Canada. Although that concept has been accepted from time to time, I am afraid that under the present administration the idea of service taking precedence over strict profit is being diminished. That is regrettable and will only serve to exacer-
3436

March 3, 1978
Railway Act
bate regional inequities and the friction that contributes to the problem of national unity.
In economic and geographic terms this country does not make sense. We have tried to combine various regions of North America on an east-west axis, when all lines of geography, communication and trade run on a north-south axis. We are going against the natural trend in trying to get an entity called "Canada" together by combining east and west. It is essential, therefore, that our transportation system be strong and vital in order to preserve the fragile unity that we hold to be Canada. It is important that we have a transportation policy that does not exacerbate the division between east and west but that helps bind the country together. Where this breaks down, of course, is in the way the government has designed transportation policy. It assumes that competition is essential to an efficient transportation system and that through competition prices will be reduced and more efficiency result to the benefit of the consumer.
Another key objective of competition is to maximize profits. We run into this dilemma when we try to apply the concept of free enterprise or maximum profits to a transportation system. If that is the primary goal, and a transportation system begins to lose money on a certain section of its operations, the logic of free enterprise and the idea of user-pay demand that service on the section that is losing money be reduced or disbanded. In an ordinary business operation, the consequences of such action are usually not too severe to the consumer, as another business will take up the slack. With transportation, however, another mode of transportation is not immediately available to the area affected. If you tear up a railway line you cannot assume that an efficient highway or air service will come in to move goods and people.
The dilemma is whether you leave regions and communities isolated or with reduced transportation service in order to balance the books or make a profit. If we followed that philosophy, which I hear again and again from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in his talk about user-pay and phasing out losing parts of a transportation system, then we would contribute to national disunity. It would exacerbate the problems of people in Atlantic Canada, in northern Ontario and in parts of western Canada.
Surely we should look at our transportation system as a means of bonding the country together, as a means of removing the inequalities faced in less developed regions or regions with less natural advantages than others. I know what it is like. I come from a relatively disadvantaged region of northern Ontario where we rely on resource based industries. We have to cope with a freight rate structure that discriminates against us and prevents us from becoming independent of mining and forestry as our sources of employment and business. We cannot get secondary industry into northern Ontario, as is the case in Atlantic Canada, because freight rates discriminate against the movement of manufactured goods from secondary industry.

Freight rates are designed to move raw materials cheaply to parts of southern Ontario or to the United States where they are manufactured and resold to us as finished goods. It is always cheaper to move that kind of bulk material in its raw or semi-processed form than it is to move manufactured goods to other parts of Canada. That, of course, means that so long as we have those discriminatory freight rates we will not solve the perennial problem of boom-bust economy or high unemployment in these regions of Canada which cannot attract secondary manufacturing industries.
That is a long-term problem which has never been solved by the government. It could be solved if this bill went further than it did. The bill should look at the totality of railway transportation and financing and bring about a rationalization of the system. If the bill brought about an amalgamation of the CNR and CPR into one publicly owned and directed Crown corporation so that we could end these persistent anomalies, the problems of freight rate discrimination which continue to give advantage to certain parts of the country and disadvantage to other parts could be solved.
The community of Sault Ste. Marie has the Algoma Steel Corporation. Steel is manufactured goods, and one would assume we could move it to any part of Canada and be able to compete in the market. However, we found that freight rates work in a reverse sense, even on some of our manufactured goods. Most recently we found that it is cheaper for the steel fabricators of British Columbia to use steel produced in Japan, transported across the Pacific Ocean and landed in British Columbia. That steel is moved more cheaply than by moving steel from Algoma along the railway system to British Columbia.
Indeed, Algoma Steel has experimented with putting the steel on ships moving it through the St. Lawrence seaway, via the Atlantic Ocean, the Panama canal, the Pacific Ocean and along the coast of British Columbia. This was an attempt to discover if this method is a less costly way of moving steel to the west coast than by putting in on flatcars and transporting it by rail. What a ridiculous situation, Mr. Speaker, that we are forced into that kind of long sea route in order to land goods on the west coast of Canada so as to compete with foreign steel. It points out the problem of rail transportation in this country.
We have heard from western members in this House of Commons as to how they can never get manufactured goods out to their part of the country cheaply, or indeed set up factories in the west and move goods to the east. That is certainly a problem that the refinancing of the CNR is not going to solve. I fault the government for not bringing in a more comprehensive transportation policy in this sense.
We have to look not only at freight and the movement of it but at the movement of people by a passenger service. Those of us who live in sparsely populated parts of Canada are worried about the changes that are being made by the government in rail transportation. We know the new transportation system called VIA Rail will soon be in effect. That has meant
March 3, 1978

reducing parts of the transcontinental service on the CNR line through northern Ontario. Certainly the small communities that service that passenger train will feel the effects of its reduction in lay-offs of railway workers.
My community has felt the effects of the transport minister's attempt to cut back on his budget by cutting back on subsidies paid to the railways on their passenger rail service. The passenger service between Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury no longer exists because of the government's decision a year or so ago. Again we find ourselves discriminated against because of this irrational policy. We know rail passenger service has a good future in this country in terms of its energy efficiency as well as in its cost of moving people. Yet this government seems so preoccupied with air service, with tremendous capital investment going into airport expansion et cetera to the neglect of designing a fast and efficient rail service.
We see a similar kind of policy by the present government that discriminates against smaller communities as a result of cutbacks in its transportation budget. I think of the question I raised today with the Minister of Transport on the government's attempt to reduce the operation of the ship canal and the lock at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario. We have been waiting for months now for the final decision of the government on whether it will spend money to improve and upgrade this lock. We can then continue to have our workers employed and continue to have the $1 million worth of revenue or more the lock generates and that is pumped into the economy of Sault Ste. Marie.
When I think of the new evidence we have before us of increased coal shipments from western Canada to Thunder Bay, and then via ship to the St. Lawrence Seaway, it would appear to me this is an argument not to let the Canadian lock continue to be degraded and to lose its commercial viability. Here we should be thinking of expanding and upgrading it and building a new superlock at Sault Ste. Marie to handle this increased tonnage which will result from the increased coal shipments through the St. Lawrence Seaway system.
All these factors point to a transportation system that is not developing on a rational basis. It seems to me that this bill only goes part way in trying to make the CNR more viable. I say we should have a comprehensive piece of legislation which looks at both railway systems and reorganizes and refinances them both.
We must maintain the principle that profit-taking alone cannot be the primary function of a transportation system that is by any sense national. We have to have the concept of service very high in our policy formulation, and I do not see that happening with the cutbacks and policies that this government and the minister are undertaking.
1 am concerned about the Minister of Transport promoting the concept of user-pay. In the smaller areas we do not have the volume of use, either through the movement of freight or the passenger service, that can justify the service receiving enough revenue solely from those who use it. They will have to continue with subsidies to the various rail and other transportation systems in order that small communities which do not
Railway Act
have the volume can still have that essential service in their daily lives.
Any movement toward a strict concept of making a system viable only on the concept of revenues generated from those who use it will surely exacerbate the problem in the various regions of Canada. 1 am concerned too that part of the thinking by the minister in moving this bill was shown in his statement that at times we should sell off the more profitable parts of the CNR to private industry. He implied that once we make certain sections profitable the government should not be concerned with managing and operating those sections. They would then be attractive to private investors and we should sell off parts of our Crown corporation to them. If we move in that direction, we will be in the predicament I mentioned at the beginning of my speech.
If private operators buy the profitable parts of CN, their way of thinking and primary policy will be that their operation must always make a profit. If there are times when that operation begins to lose money, the private operator, working on the principles of free enterprise, and I do not fault him because only logically can he come to this conclusion, will reduce parts of that service in order to make a profit. That will mean certain areas of the country will be disadvantaged.
The history of transportation in this country has shown that we have to keep the concept of service on an equal footing with the concept of sound business operations in an attempt to have a most efficient and, where possible, profitable operation. Therefore I have to conclude that only by maintaining public control over our transportation system can we guarantee for all Canadians, no matter where they live, that the concept of essential service will be maintained.
In a sense, the bill is a bit of a move in the right direction in trying to reduce the burden of debt that the CNR is facing. However, I worry about what this means for the future in terms of over-all transportation plans of this government and this minister. As I stated before, my fear is that we will end up with a transportation system that does not bind our country together, providing equality of service and opportunity, but one that gives advantages to certain parts of the country because they are more blessed with markets and resources than other parts. No government worth its salt can move in that direction if it is serious about national unity and developing a sound economy.
With those reservations, we will support the bill, but we will be watching very carefully and be very critical of the minister if he moves in the direction of reducing service and privatizing parts of this very important Crown corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to make some comments on this bill at the second reading stage. First I want to commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) for bringing this bill before the House. It is not very voluminous but indeed it will have
80033 -SJ/2

March 3, 1978
Railway Act
far-reaching consequences for the whole country. I think everybody had been expecting such a bill for a long time; we have been expecting it for many years, and I figure it is a good start towards a reorganization of our rail services throughout Canada. Also 1 want to say that unlike some of the previous speakers of the opposition, I will not begin my comments by saying that the government favours one province over another, or Montreal over Winnipeg, or Toronto over some other city in some other province. In my opinion, that is not the way to enter the debate, because if I speak favourably of the bill, I will do so talking about my region since it is the only one I know, just as people from western Canada do not know much about Quebec when telling us whether they are for or against the bill.
I will not say a word about other regions because I know people out west also have needs. They have to talk about their needs but not to the extent of running down or belittling certain needs in some other province they know nothing about. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I will limit my comments to my area and what the bill will mean for it. You can be sure that we support the bill wholeheartedly. This bill is entitled: "An Act to amend the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act and the Railway Act and to amend and repeal certain other statutes in consequence thereof'. In summary, Bill C-17 provides in Section 6:
. . . would authorize the Governor in Council to cancel not more than eight hundred and eight million dollars of debt owned by the Company to the Crown, together with any interest falling due thereon after December 31st, 1977 . ..
And Section 7, I quote:
. . . would provide for the surrender to the Company for cancellation of all four per cent preferred stock held by the Minister of Finance on December 31st, 1977.
And finally, and I quote:
Section 9 would establish the authorized and issued capital stock of the National Company at six million common shares of no par value and provide for the value those shares are to have in the accounts of the Company.
In return, the CN shall pay the Receiver General of Canada a dividend of 20 per cent, which will leave it, finally, with 80 per cent to manage the company business. In short, Bill C-17 simply cancels the debt of the Canadian National with the government-capital and interest-roughly $20 billion, in order for the company to get back on an even keel.
Often the people are misled for lack of an explanation. Unfortunately, when a member puts pertinent questions trying to better enlighten the people, the government, through the minister responsible, often answers that it is a matter of internal administration for the Crown company and that it cannot give out the information requested. The people wonder, and rightly so, why the CN ends up in the red every year whereas CP reports net profits at the end of each fiscal year. Would it be easier to control the expenditures and the administration of a private company than those of a Crown corporation? Would it be that in a private company there are officials
(Mr. Gauthier (Robcrval).]
who have a financial interest to protect whereas in a Crown corporation there are no such people in fact and that the directors have just their salary to protect? But I shall not be that sadistic.
I owe explanations to the population, and the government should give these explanations it has in fact. We only have to check the CN balance sheet to see that the deficit of the administration would not be so high if it were not for the interests which take out a good part of its budget. The CN has in fact an operating surplus. But the CN has an old debt accrued over years, on which it pays interest which are too high. I see the reason for these loans in the fact that we force CN to maintain deficit producing lines in remote areas. 1 would even say that very often CN plays the part of a stop-gap. Where CP does not want to venture or withdraws because it is not as profitable as they expected, CN is ordered to go by the government. Therefore it is the government which is in fact responsible for this deficit. And to make things worse, the same government requires CN to pay interest on these loans instead of simply subsidizing it. There should be at least special supplementary assistance in non-profitable areas but, instead of that, CN has to borrow from the government and when it gets free assistance, CP takes equal advantage of this government assistance to transportation.
1 think it is a kind of underhand protectionism towards CP. All this passes unnoticed. Both companies get subsidies as if both had the obligation to serve profitable as well as non-profitable areas. But if we look at our two railway systems, we realize that CN has to serve undeveloped and remote areas much more often than CP. We should beware of this in the new organization.
I also believe that over-centralization is one of the reasons for the CN deficit. I remember that when there was a minor breakdown on an engine, in my Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean area, it had to be sent to Montreal to be repaired, even if it meant just an hour, an hour and a half or two hours of work. Can you imagine that? The engine had to be sent to Montreal for repairs which meant 32, 36 or 40 hours before it was back. Then they put in servo-centres to follow the moves of coaches and know at every moment where each of them was.
It is all very well to sit in an office and admire the movement of railway cars, but what is important is that these cars can travel in all safety on the railroad. And for that, it is necessary to have adequate maintenance personnel, not people who sit in offices. This is of no use when it comes to repairing the railroads, Mr. Speaker. And there are now too many people in the offices and not enough on the lines. I believe that 50 per cent of all derailments which have caused losses amounting to millions of dollars in the last few years could have been avoided had there been maintenance teams on location and had there been enough employees to maintain the railroads. 1 hope that the new organization will create new maintenance sectors.
March 3, 1978

As concerns decentralization, I believe that we have just made a giant step by creating two separate organizations for the transport of goods and the transport of passengers. We are therefore very happy about the creation of VIA Rail and we have high expectations about this new agency, this new VIA Rail company as concerns quality and service. I hope that in all meetings and discussions, priority will be given to the quality of service instead of profitability. Those appointed are already at work.
I have been able to speak with a few of them and I can tell you that they seem quite prepared to provide adequate passenger service in our area of the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean. If we have a modernized transportation network, well-maintained railways, orderly traffic, priority of passengers over freight and schedules acceptable for the majority of customers, you can be sure that the estimates of those now responsible will be met, that is doubling the number of users in two years. This is what the promoters now want to do.
I have assured them that they will be surprised if they do as they now plan because there are customers waiting for this service in our area. Our area has a population of more than 300,000, which means that there are many potential customers for an adequate service. I have always urged consultation with the local authorities, otherwise, the population of the Sague-nay-Lac-Saint-Jean will lose interest. I am now certain that the dialogue will be helpful for the expansion of VIA Rail and to provide more adequate service to our population. Of course, we are satisfied with Bill C-17 and we would like it to be referred as soon as possible to the standing committee of the House so that it may be studied in depth and improved if required to provide better service and improved safety.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on Bill C-17 today I will begin by pointing out that those ribbons of steel which run into northern Manitoba known as the CN rail lines are really the basis of the economic life and future of my part of the country. I think of the line which runs from the top of Lynn Lake to carry out iron ore and serve the communities along the route. I think, too, of the 500-mile line which runs from Le Pas to Churchill. The rail lines in northern Manitoba are just like milk to a baby. Without them our economic future would be bleak indeed.
I see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is here. I know he is interested in the Port of Churchill and is following this discussion with interest. The bill before us was introduced in the House on December 19, 1977. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) urged the opposition to pass it immediately. Its effect will be to cancel, as of December 31, 1977, $808 million of debt owed by the CN to the government. According to the Minister of Transport this would give the company a capital structure appropriate to a mature corporation and provide it with a realistic debt-equity ratio.
Railway Act
After the recapitalization of 1952, the debt-equity ratio of the company was comparable to that of the Canadian Pacific. But since 1952 CN has been carrying a huge debt burden, though in different circumstances, CP rail has earned a profit every year and never missed a dividend.
This is the third time the CNR has come to parliament asking to be relieved of debt. The Prime Minister is asking us to pass quickly a bill which will erase CN's debt to the people, for the third time. That will put a service in the black which belongs in the red. How can the government expect taxpayers to refinance a transportation system which causes only frustration and hardship, which reorganizes attitudes and services to improve profit ratio, only to become more inefficient and inoperable?
In 1974 the transport committee promised CN $20 million for rebuilding the railway from Gillam to Churchill. When the Hudson Bay Railway was constructed, 80 pound steel was used, that is, 80 pounds per foot steel. What has been taking place over the past number of years is the upgrading of this rail line to 100 pound steel in order to enable trains to carry heavier carloads and so on.
The line which commences at Gillam, Manitoba, has now been upgraded as far as the Herchmer subdivision. The balance of that rail for 200 miles is 80 pound steel, which is causing a real problem with the movement of grain, especially to the Port of Churchill. This is because of the 100 ton hopper cars which are being used. In spile of the rail facilities into Churchill, fortunately last year during the grain shipping season there were very, very few accidents on this particular part of the line. I give a lot of credit to the running crews who have a dedication and responsibility to get grain to Churchill. They attempted to set an all-time record of some 30 million bushels. This was not quite achieved for the simple reason that two of the last ships, which were to haul grain out of Churchill, did not arrive. They were diverted to Montreal.
The rail was to be upgraded to the tune of $20 million. It was to be completed by 1978. Due to a problem as to jurisdiction or classification of the remaining mileage which required upgrading, the entire plan fell by the wayside. On that same piece between Gillam and Churchill, there is no passing track in that 173 miles. That means trains leaving Churchill and heading back into Gillam must complete the run before they meet another loaded train which is going to Churchill. It is important for the lifeblood of the north, Churchill, and that entire 510 miles of line that this last portion be upgraded to 100 pound steel in order to eliminate the possibility of severe spills because of light rail; and also in order to be able to accommodate the 100 ton hopper cars which are now being used for the transportation of grain.
In 1978 northerners are still not sure whether this portion of track will be upgraded. There could be something in the estimates at this particular time, but I have not seen any indication that the line will be upgraded to accommodate the new aluminum hopper cars which will be replacing CN's fleet

March 3, 1978
Railway Act
that is presently handling grain. If the track is not upgraded in order to handle hopper cars, then the entire mechanism of hopper car dumping at the Port of Churchill will be thrown out. The present system was designed for dumping boxcars. By 1986 boxcars will no longer be used, and only hopper cars will be used to transport grain.
This should be a priority of CN. The remaining 173 miles should be upgraded. Actually, it is closer to 180 miles of track between Gillam and Churchill. It is a case of trying to sort out the priorities of the government as to which project should be carried out. When one looks at the potential of this 510 miles of railway to northern Manitoba and many parts of Saskatchewan, where the grain is produced which is shipped through the Port of Churchill, then one realizes it must be a priority. 1 hope the government will make an announcement. It would be a good area to be included in an election campaign, that is, the completion of that 180 miles of rail with 100 pound steel. It would not gain the Minister of Transport any votes, but certainly it would assist the economy of that particular area. Since the Minister of Transport comes from Saskatchewan, I am sure he will be interested in satisfying some of the grain producers who ship through Port Churchill by upgrading the track.
The Hall Commission report recommended very strongly that the government immediately upgrade the 180 miles of track in the Herchmer subdivision north of Gillam. Also it was recommended that it be designated development, rather than a grain dependent line. This is where the problem arose: the interpretation of development or grain dependent line. This is where the problem still lies. As far as 1 know, it still has not been ratified.
Originally CN assumed this line would be eligible for federal subsidies. They had already invested $6 million in upgrading some parts of the line. Some 85 per cent of the traffic on this particular line is for the Port of Churchill in line with the grain handling, yet CN cannot justify a further expenditure of $15 million which is necessary for the completion of the line. I cannot understand the rationale here.

speechtext:
Just prior to one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was talking about the upgrading of the rail line between Gillam and Churchill from 80 pound to 100 pound steel. Considering the investment the CNR and the government have made in respect of the railway, the town and the port of
[Mr. Smith (Churchill).J
Churchill, it seems to me that to stop now when a total of two thirds of the job is completed just does not wash. I cannot understand how the government can justify spending that large amount of money to upgrade certain portions and then, all of a sudden, stop the project because of a change in policy or a change in heart.
What does this upgrading of the railway facility really mean to the port of Churchill? I suggest it means the life or death of that port, and I would ask the government to give very serious consideration to putting up the money to finish this upgrading process, because Churchill is a viable grain handling port and, in fact, has the most efficient grain handling operation in Canada. That has been clearly spelled out.
Let me point out that the government, in its wisdom and planning, has just spent something like $50 million to redevelop the town of Churchill, including an $11 million expenditure on a recreation complex. No one is really arguing about whether this upgrading is essential, but at the present time, due to government cutbacks in Churchill, with a reduction in the number of people working for the National Research Council and the CBC, following its pull-out, Churchill is now left with a total population of about 1,500 people. They can no longer afford the upkeep on an $11 million recreation complex.
The CNR has refused to commit the final expenditure on the line between Gillam and Churchill because it does not appear profitable to them, and the reason is that the government will not give a decision to CNR on what the future of the port of Churchill will be. Of course this jeopardizes everyone's livelihood and leaves people in the area with a feeling of exasperation and helplessness, not really knowing what their future will be. They thought there was a future there when they saw the line upgraded, when they saw the community redevelopment program and $50 million spent there. That gave them some hope that there was a future, but unless that line is upgraded there will be absolutely no future.
I want to get into another area regarding cutbacks and what has happened in the CNR. Perhaps what 1 will talk about should be classified as cutbacks, but let me comment on how the redevelopment or the reorganization of the CNR has affected northern Manitoba and the Churchill constituency.
At one time northern Manitoba produced some of the best fresh fish in Canada. This included whitefish, pickerel, and jackfish. At that time all fish were shipped out on CN rail. What we have seen taking place over the past couple of years has put this industry in jeopardy, and all because of increased freight rates. The communities out there do not have an opportunity to transport their goods by any means other than by rail. They are totally dependent on the railway. There are no roads leading to them and only the odd one has a small airstrip which it can use for emergency services. So what has happened?
Some 250 to 300 fishermen are now out of work for the simple reason that they can no longer afford to ship their fish by rail. It seems to me that the railway is bound and deter-
March 3, 1978

rained, I suppose following the minister's user-pay concept, to stop serving them. However, there are certain circumstances in which it is the obligation of a corporation such as the CNR to provide service to areas requiring it. Therefore they should be providing this service to the communities.
I should like to give you some examples. In 1974, continental whitefish sold for 24 cents a pound, or maybe in some cases a cent or two less. At that time the freight rate from Ilford, Manitoba, to Winnipeg was 11.33 cents a pound. This left the fishermen 12.67 cents a pound for themselves. On January 20, 1975, the fish was still selling on the market for 24 cents a pound. This was the Fresh Water Fish Marketing Corporation in Winnipeg. But freight rates jumped to 12.18 cents a pound for the same fish. On May 5 of the same year, with prices unchanged, the freight rate has increased to 14.3 cents a pound. This left the fishermen 9.7 cents a pound, an amount which made it virtually impossible for them to meet their commitments. But until that time at least, the CNR would transport the fish, even though the fishermen could no longer afford to transport the fish.
At today's fish prices and with the increased cost of transportation, northern commercial fishermen are hard pressed even to pay for their food bills, let alone to pay for their equipment. We must realize that the railway provides the only link that many of these communities have with the outside world, and when the Hudson Bay Railway built the railway- it was completed to Churchill in 1931-someone had a concept regarding the development of the economy in the area and serving the small communities that had sprung up because of the railway.
What we have seen happening in the fishing industry is an increase in prices, so the fishermen got together and started to ship larger shipments of fish, in that way achieving a more reasonable rate for the shipments, carload lots, and so on. Also, what fishermen had to do was to go to the province of Manitoba, which is now paying a freight subsidy in order to keep these fishermen working. When the freight subsidy was put into effect, fishermen could survive on the return they were getting after freight. But lo and behold, in 1977, the CNR, in their wisdom, tried to cut costs and services as much as they possibly could. This case was brought here to the floor of the House of Commons and to the minister, as well as in committee. What had taken place was that an arbitrary decision was made by someone-certainly not someone in northern Manitoba-that the railway would stop hauling fresh fish. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, how quickly this decision was put into place.
A fisherman at Arnaud, which is about mile 237 on the Hudson Bay Railway, had been out commercial fishing in the fall and had made some shipments of fish. He arrived at the track at 3.30 one morning to load his fish on to the train which comes from Churchill to the spot where he can put it on a truck and move it to Winnipeg by that means. However, he was at Arnaud where usually he is forced to load his fish on the train because there is no other means of transportation. This time when he arrived at the train at 3.30 in the morning-here is a man who is trying to make a living doing
Railway Act
something he has done all his life-he was told by the conductor, "I am sorry, we have been issued orders now that we are not to haul any more fish."
The train left and the fisherman was left standing on the side of the track with his 35 boxes of fresh fish. We all know that fresh fish must be kept fresh if it is to ever reach the consumer in an edible state. Can you imagine what that has done to the fisherman! We have the highest unemployment in northern Manitoba next to that in Newfoundland. This fellow was so dejected that he was ready to quit right there and go on welfare, collect unemployment insurance, or do something else.
1 am citing this one example but there are many, many other examples such as this. However, through efforts made in the House of Commons, talking to the minister and getting in touch with the regional people of the CNR, we were successful in getting that fish picked up by the next train two days later. This meant that the fish had to be held on ice for that length of time. However, the fisherman was able to complete his fishing season.
We thought that everything was in place and that the CNR would continue to transport fish. When I went to CNR officials and presented the problem to them, the answer that 1 received was, "We are sorry, we do not have any facilities or any equipment for hauling fish". 1 said, "Sirs, you have been hauling fish out of Manitoba since that rail line has existed, so don't give me that hogwash because it certainly does not wash with me." This is the attitude which seems to be taken every day now. When services are cut back, it is hoped that people will not say too much, but those ribbons of steel which go into northern Manitoba are the economic future not only of Manitoba but of much of the rest of Canada.
When we consider the extraction of Arctic gas and oil which is taking place we must bear in mind that these rail lines will be very important. Road construction in the north at today's prices and because of muskeg and permafrost costs about $1.5 million to $1.75 million per mile.
When I spoke about the 250 to 300 fishermen affected by the increase in freight rates and the refusal to handle fish, I did not mention other people who are put out of work. People on shore who handle fish, packers and others, are involved. Seven hundred people are actually affected just along that portion of track alone.
This is not the only cutback we have seen. Recently it was arbitrarily decided to discontinue the service at Pikwitoni, which is a small community of about 350 people. It was decided to take the agent out of that community. There are no banks there. The people there depend entirely on the CNR to send money orders out. Many of the people have their groceries brought in by the railway. With no agent there a person cannot buy a ticket to get on the train. There is no one there to receive any shipments, but a dear price is charged for shipments into that community whether those shipments contain oil for stoves, gas for boats, which are used for fishing, or groceries.

Railway Act
When the decision was made to close Pikwitoni, people argued desperately for the retention of the agent so that their goods could be received. However, in the wisdom of whoever it is who decides, the station was closed.
As recently as February, 1978, a decision was made by CNR not to close places like Ilford, Thicket Portage, Cranberry Portage and Sherridon. That decision was arrived at after some consultation with those communities. At first it was decided to close those stations, but then the CNR went to the various communities and held meetings. 1 want to compliment those communities because their mayors, councils and advisory committees met with officials from the CNR. They presented a good case and told the railway in no uncertain terms that those stations should remain intact and that the agents should remain at those stations, not only for the good of the communities but also for the simple reason that it would be a safety measure if trains would actually use the track. It is good for those communities to have someone to handle the goods being shipped in and out.
I would like to read some of the comments of the mayor of Thicket Portage when it was decided to withdraw these services from the community of Thicket Portage, as follows:
Dear Cec.,
We listened to your recent broadcast outlining the joys of having the CNR increase its grain shipments through the Port of Churchill. . .
I was referring then to the Hall Commission report.
In order to provide some goodies to northerners the CNR was saying it would increase grain shipments to Churchill. At least that is what the Hall Commission report said, but I do not know how we are going to get this government to act on some of the Hall Commission recommendations. In a statement not too long ago the Minister of Transport said he had still not determined whether the Port of Churchill is a viable operation.
The mayor of Thicket Portage went on in his letter to explain how discouraging it is for a community which is totally dependent on the railway. Thicket Portage is a community of some 400 people. It has started a market gardening project so that it can ship vegetables to other communities in the north. This is a first for Thicket Portage and a first for the north. The community did not know what to do with the goods it produced, because if there was no agent at the station, there would be no way to load goods onto trains. One shipment of potatoes was made. The shipment had to go only 55 miles, but that took two weeks. By the time the potatoes arrived they were sprouted and soft, but the full rate had to be paid. There was no discount.
The mayor also pointed out that when the CNR was first established in that part of the country, people became totally dependent on it. They have no other means of transportation. The mayor of Thicket Portage lives in the north. He and many other people have survived there for a number of years. They are trying desperately to find jobs. They are not satisfied with living on welfare and on Canada Works projects. They want to contribute to the tax base of this country. I for one can vouch that people in the north are able to work and want to work. I
[Mr. Smith (Churchill).l
wish I had the time to read this whole letter from Mayor Bob McCleverty of Thicket Portage, because it is a masterpiece.
Circumstances similar to the ones I have just outlined jeopardize living in northern Manitoba. As I said before, the CNR is to blame for much of this because it does not appear that there is any consultation with the communities involved whatsoever. Arbitrary decisions are made and people become involved after the fact. It is about time the CNR and the government realized that we have more than polar bears in the constituency of Churchill. We also have many people who are very concerned Canadians and who want to contribute to Canadian society.
I would like to speak about a couple of fishermen at Pukatawagan. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you do not know just where that is, but it is about 99 miles north of the Pas on the way to Lynn Lake. The people of Pukatawagan must move from lake to lake on the CNR. They have no choice. In this particular case these fishermen loaded their two boats onto the train and were transported about 35 miles. The fishermen unloaded the two boats themselves. They received a bill from the CNR for $294, or 1.96 cents per pound. In the face of that how can people who depend on the railway and who have no other means of transportation possibly survive? They just give up in frustration. They wonder what is the sense of trying to do anything. Because of some new policy regarding cubic footage, if a person has a full carload he must pay on that basis. It does not matter whether you have one box of fish or fifty-you pay the same price. That is fine if you are gathering from a large area, but many of these fishermen gather from a very small area and this sort of thing is hard on them.
The mayor of Ilford, Manitoba, Mr. Kip Thompson, depends totally on the CNR, and if I had time to read some of his letters into the record 1 am sure they would bring this government down tomorrow.

Of course the government is coming down very shortly anyway. One way to make sure to get rid of them would be to put them all on a train to Churchill.
Ilford, Manitoba, is a centre for shipping goods to places like Oxford House, Split Lake or York Landing. What has happened over the years is that the CNR delivers the cars to a siding where the goods are unloaded and then transported inland. In the last two years whole carloads of goods have been lost on that 510-mile railway. Mr. Speaker, they do not run off the track into the bush. Many of the goods lost are perishables.
I should like the government to check on the demurrage charges and the claims along the Hudson Bay Railway because I am sure the amount paid out is astronomical. There does not seem to be the will to deliver a piece of equipment or a box of groceries intact-any more. It seems as if the CNR is doing everything in its power to discourage people from using it but, of course, where there is no other means of transporta-
March 3, 1978

tion, people have to use this line in order to get the goods through.
The Railway Transport Committee Order No. R-25988 reads in part as follows:
IN THE MATTER OF the application of the Canadian National Railways to discontinue their passenger-train service between Winnipeg, Thompson and Churchill, in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, comprising Train Numbers 90, 91, 92-94, and 93-95,
The next paragraph begins the same way and continues as follows:
. . . passenger-train service between Wabowden and Gillam and between Gillam and Churchill, in the Province of Manitoba, comprising Train Numbers 294 and 295,
It goes on in the next paragraph:
. . . between The Pas and Lynn Lake, in the Province of Manitoba, comprising Train Numbers 290 and 291, and
The next one reads:

What this amounts to is an application to discontinue the passenger service into northern Manitoba in total. Thank goodness the committee decided that the trains that ran between The Pas and Lynn Lake, The Pas and Churchill and also up to Osborne Lake, should not be discontinued. Even though the CN pointed out that they are running at a deficit, they are still providing an essential service. There is an obligation on the Crown corporation to provide these services even though they may be operating at a loss for the time being. Perhaps the present type of service is not the best one and we should be looking for a better and faster means of transportation such as dayliners and other things.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank you for giving me time to point out why I feel the bill should be discussed. 1 think people from all parts of the country should give their views on the recapitalization of the CNR.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us this afternoon Bill C-17 which has come to be known as the CNR bill. The main thrust of the bill is the removal of some $800 million of debt from the CNR. This does not eliminate the debt, however, because before the bill came down there was a long term debt of $2,238,000 of which there is $1,438,000 remaining.
The minister said in this House that this $800 million debt should be removed so that he will not have to come back to the House for regular assistance to the CNR. A number of years ago a debt was removed which was supposed to fix things so that the government would never have to come back to the House requesting assistance for the CNR, and over the years there has been a total tax relief of debt to the CNR of some $6.7 billion. I would not be too unhappy about that if we had a transportation system, especially in western Ontario and the Atlantic provinces, doing what is necessary to enhance transportation in this country. Instead, we find the CNR trying to follow the lead of its competitor, the CPR, which has become
Railway Act
one of the biggest industries in Canada although not completely in the field of transportation. The CPR is widely and strongly assisted by the coffers of the federal government which, of course, means the taxpayers of Canada.
We had a prize example when the CN tried to build one of the biggest edifices in Canada, the CN Tower in Toronto. Large amounts of money were probably blown which really did not have anything at all to do with transportation in Canada. CN has other similar interests. It has tried to follow the CPR. But it is not really providing a rail service of transportation that we need in Canada. It should not be trying to follow the CPR. It should be out showing the CPR what transportation is all about. It should be an example for transportation in Canada. It should become the best. It should be doing all of the things necessary to become one of the top transportation companies in North America.
1 have to say that I think CN management have fallen into the same trap that government bureaucrats do. They have become top heavy at the executive level. They have not really put out the effort which is necessary in the transportation field and that is vital to Canada. We have many transportation problems in western Canada. Whenever we have a first ministers' meeting it is one of the top items on the agenda as far as the western premiers and the premiers from the Atlantic provinces are concerned.
Last year I travelled with the transport committee into the Atlantic provinces. I was astounded to find the same problems exist in Atlantic Canada that exist in western Canada. The railways were charging what the traffic would bear. This is the way they use what we might call "the two ends of Canada". They charge whatever rates the traffic will bear, whatever they can get. There is neither rhyme nor reason to their transportation rates.
There is an obligation on the railways because of the large amounts of money which have been transferred from the taxpayers to the CNR and, of course, to the CPR over the years. They have an obligation to ensure that we have a good and proper transportation system in Canada.
I have a brief here that was written by the Canadian Transport Commission concerning the fruit industry of the Okanagan valley. Over the years the Okanagan valley has been under the gun from the transportation companies because they charged and they still charge what the traffic will bear. They do not begin to compete with their railway counterparts in the United States, bearing in mind that the fruit producer, the farmer, has to compete with the producer in the United States. Apples are allowed to enter Canada duty free. There is no tariff. We do not mind this sort of thing. It is only when we find ourselves being discriminated against as far as charges are concerned as well as some of the other related industry costs that we begin to wonder what is happening to us.
We have made many representations to the railways, and quite a few to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). We have made them to the Canadian Transport Commission. This is a

fairly thick document but it does not really say too much about transportation. That, Mr. Speaker, is in my opinion what the CTC should be concerned about. They spend more time telling the fruit growers in the Okanagan valley what is wrong with them. They are not really researching to find out what is in effect wrong with the transportation companies, wrong with the rates, and wrong with the charges that we have imposed on us by the CNR and the CPR in freight rates. It was so frustrating to the fruit growers because of the difference in rates between the Canadian railways and the American railways that they have practically turned to truck transportation.
A few years ago I was heavily involved in that industry, and with the agreed charges on rail rates we had to consent to send 60 to 70 per cent of our produce over the railways to get a lower rate. What happened was the railways would not, did not, could not supply the cars. They did not hold up their end of the bargain. They were the ones who said, "If you want a lower rate we will have an agreed charge. You must agree to send most of your product through us". But they could not deliver the goods when it came right down to it. They did not have any intention to deliver. We had frustration after frustration. We saw our competitors' produce coming into western Canada and going into our export markets. We were not able to compete because the transportation facilities were not there.
When I look at the $6.7 billion which the taxpayers have transferred to the CNR over the years I wonder why they have not been able to deliver the goods and become a top transportation company in Canada. That is one example. There are many other examples in western Canada of exactly the same kind of treatment that industry producers and farm products have received. We can talk about them over and over again. A former minister of transport got up in this House and I was here when he did so, threw up his hands, and said that transportation in Canada is in a mess. He was right.

speechtext:
My colleague from Calgary North says they sent him to the Senate. That is exactly what happened. That is exactly what he got for identifying the fact that transportation was in a mess. Then they brought in the big man from Saskatchewan to become the Minister of Transport. He is pretty good at covering up; however, we do not have a better transportation system. We are not getting better service. Nothing is any better than it was before, even though the Minister of Transport said the other day that the mess in transportation in Canada has been cleaned up.
I do not know who the minister is trying to fool. 1 do not know why he would try to kid the people of Canada unless it is because there will soon be an election.
Every time 1 fly into Vancouver 1 can see 22 vessels in the harbour waiting to be loaded with grain. It is great that we have these grain sales. Without them, our balance of trade deficit would be much greater. Our imports would be much greater. Grain is the one item that makes our agricultural

exports look good. However, it is deplorable that the grain cannot be delivered to the harbour at Vancouver and that the ships must wait there. They must pay demurrage costs of up to $500 a day. Who pays that? It is the farmer of western Canada. This is only because the transportation companies cannot make their deliveries.
If the mess has been cleaned up, why did the Liberal premier of Nova Scotia say to the minister, "For God's sake, forget user pay", something the minister has been pushing very hard? He is transferring $800 million in debt from the CNR and then talking about user pay. Over the years this has involved $6.7 billion of the taxpayer's money. Instead of user pay, why not do what is necessary to deliver the wheat from the prairie provinces to the coast?
Why did the western premiers circumvent the Minister of Transport and call on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to implement the crucial provisions of the Hall report? Of course they were rebuffed by the Prime Minister.
The other day we heard what wonderful things the Liberal government is doing with the Hall report. Of 90 recommendations, it is going to implement five or six. The government is making a lot of the fact that it might accept five or six recommendations. Is it a coincidence that the western ministers of transport are meeting with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) rather than the present Minister of Transport? The Prime Minister could not give the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce the transport portfolio because the present minister wanted to retain it. That hon. member walked across the floor from this party because he had been promised a cabinet post. He is now taking on part of the job of the Minister of Transport as well.
It is cheaper for Canadians to travel abroad than to travel within their own country. I can fly to London for less than it would cost me to fly from my home to Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member allowing me to ask a question. Today if one compares schedule fares to schedule fares, they are on a rough par. If he compares charter competition fares to charter competition fares, the rates in Canada are in fact the same as those abroad. That is an example of how we have cured a problem which previously existed.
The hon. member referred to the CNR and the capacity of the rail system, making critical comments about it. Does he recognize that just yesterday CN announced the completion of calculations for 1977, that it has carried more freight than
March 3, 1978

ever before in its history and has made the highest profit, after payment of full interest on debt, since 1943? That is further evidence he might take note of in seeing how things have changed in the last few years.

speechtext:
I thank the hon. minister for his interruption. He wanted to ask me a question, but instead made two statements. He said that if you compare air fares, you will find they are about equal. He is talking about charter flights in Canada that have just been introduced. There would be no problem for me to get a charter flight out of Canada to almost anywhere in the world. However, it would be a big problem for me to get a charter flight in Canada between my home and Ottawa. The government is only trying to kid the people into believing that it is doing something.
The minister also stated that CNR is handling more traffic today than ever before. We heard the same statement last year in committee. Canada is bigger today, with more people and more things happening than ever before. The percentages are not that great. The transportation services that are required are not being provided. I would not be a bit surprised if the figures which were released included the truck traffic which has come about as a result of both CNR and CPR buying out trucking companies and taking over that traffic. So they don't really have to keep their rail lines going. Once they get into that area of activity the cost falls mainly on the provinces and the municipalities which supply and keep up the roads.
Today the railways are hauling large quantities of coal and other products of heavy industry. The lumber industry in western Canada has picked up considerably, another development which has been helpful to the railways. But any increase in activity which has taken place is in spite of the railways, not because of them. The situation with regard to the transportation of apples is typical. We can haul our produce out of Okanagan across the border into the United States, load it into U.S. cars for transportation east and still end up with a rate which is much better than that quoted by Canadian railways. Of course, it costs us more than our competitors have to pay because they are not obliged to spend money trucking produce across the line. The brief 1 have here tells us all about that situation. It also tells us what is wrong with the fruit industry; labour costs are too high, and so on. But it does not tell us why the rates charged by the CN and the CPR are so high.
That is what the CTC's job is. It is not to tell the fruit grower what is wrong with his industry. One of the reasons that fruit growers are finding it hard to compete is the much higher rate of transportation between western Canada and cities such as Toronto and Montreal. The Commission should get down to doing its job. The Commission should take its responsibilities more seriously, take charge of what is going on and stop cozying up to the railways. As we know, the minister brought in a bill last session having a bearing on this question of supervision. He withdrew it quickly, of course, after only a few speeches had been made on the subject; maybe too many people thought that if the minister were to take the responsi-
Railway Act
bility into his own hands things would be even worse than they are now. As I see it, we need to strengthen the CTC and ensure that it does the job it is supposed to do. It is not the minister's job to become a kind of dictator in this area. If my proposal were followed, maybe we would get more sense and better service.
1 had intended to say a few words about rail line abandonment even though it is not directly involved in the bill before us. When the CN and the CP abandon rail lines, as they are prone to do, the corridors, the rights of way, should revert to the Crown. I have put forward a private member's bill on this subject. When I use the term "revert to the Crown" I have in mind the federal Crown. That is really the only way in which I can present the case to this House because, after all, we are the federal parliament. But I would have no quarrel with the idea of the rights reverting to the provincial governments or to the municipalities concerned. When I first introduced this idea to the House-and I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) would agree that I was the first to introduce it, whether he likes it or not-rights of way which had been abandoned went back to the railway companies, which meant, in effect, to one of their real estate subsidiaries; the CNR has one and Canadian Pacific has a big one. As soon as that happens, everybody had better look out.
Mr. Speaker, the corridors the railways are using today should not be closed, particularly in cities or areas where it would be very expensive to buy them back if and when the supply of fossil fuels comes to an end and we are obliged to place far better reliance on rail transportation. I do not know whether this will happen in my lifetime, probably not; but it may very well happen in the lifetime of my children or my grandchildren. Suppose the rail corridors through Penticton were sold. There would be just no way of getting them back at anything like reasonable cost. The railway companies do not care. They do not have a sense of responsibility any more, but the government will be back where it started so many years ago when it faced the responsibility of setting up communications from one end of the country to the other.
The Minister of Transport wants to make a deal with the municipalities and the provinces. I think he should warn them that if they sell off this property the responsibility for restoring it, should railway communications be needed again, should be theirs. The taxpayers of Canada as a whole should not be saddled with the cost. In my view it would be much better to make sure that these corridors are left open.
I realize it is the intention to forgive the CNR some $800 million more of its debt. 1 say to the management of the company and to the Minister of Transport: Get busy and live up to your responsibility, which is to provide good transportation. We need it desperately. We need much better service. If we have to have some shake-up in the CTC and in the management of the railways to get it, then let us do it. Let us get on with cleaning up the mess. Let us not try to kid people into thinking it is cleared up.
