speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining the debate on the bill before us, I do so not only with a national interest in mind but also with the interest of my area, the riding of York-Simcoe, very much in mind. We have lived for some time with this question of our transportation problems, and the question of inadequate ministers in the portfolio of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in this decrepit government that we have in Canada. Perhaps there is no place where the inadequacy of this government shows more than with respect to its operation of Crown corporations.
Fundamentally what the government is proposing now is the third sequence of burying previous mistakes with respect to previous activities of Crown corporations. Most of us realize that the excuse given by the government for this refinancing and recapitalization bill is that the CN is carrying too heavy a load of debt in relation to its equity, if that can be believed; and if the CN is relieved of its burden of debt, somehow it will go on to even better and more profitable heights. In short, relieve them of their debt and they will do better. That seems to be the message of the government, if one believes its spokesman and if one reads what the bill proposes.
In the few brief moments I have at my disposal I should like to touch on how that debt occurred. What in fact has caused the ratio between debt and equity which the CN now complains about? How does that ratio compare to its main competitor, CP? Why does CP happen to have a better ratio between equity and debt? I will deal with these areas in more detail shortly. The short answer is that CP has been able to make better earnings and better profits. In turn, that has allowed CP to build up its equity, which of course means less debt and a better ratio between debt and equity.
Also I should like to touch on the point why a government directed Crown corporation has to run in the loss position which we have experienced in CN over so many years. What goes wrong? What goes wrong that operations under the direction of government are not able to remain viable or profitable? It is partly because in the government's mind there is never a bottom line to the operation of a Crown corporation. There is never any feeling that somehow that operation, if it is to run efficiently, probably should be showing a profit.
The basic ingredient found in most businesses in the private sector is that those who invest expect to make a profit on their investments. If they do not, they start asking where the inadequacies are. They demand changes and they get changes. In short order, if they are running substantial losses, they are bankrupt. The reason I refer to this is that we deal in government in a never-never land. The government of the day for political expediency, as has been followed by the Trudeau government so religiously, agrees to non-viable ventures or activities, realizing that money will be lost, but somehow having a vague feeling that the results will be buried in the over-all estimates for the cost of government doing business and that no one will feel the pinch. The hard fact is we all eventually feel the pinch.

The pinch we are feeling was dramatically brought out during oral questions today. We asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) a very simple question. We asked him what he proposed to do to reverse the balance of payments deficit in this country, which has been running chronically in a deficit position since 1973. Also we ask him what he intends to do to reverse that position, which is causing our dollar to collapse on international markets and is causing us to borrow more and more funds that will have to be repaid, including interest, some day. The Minister of Finance did not have the slightest suggestion to give to the House as to how he proposed to correct that fundamental error. He could have suggested that he would start running some of our activities, such as the CN in a more efficient manner. He could have suggested making them more productive in order for them to deliver better service to their clientele, at the same time as saving Canadians a huge amount of outgo in loss.
It is very, very nice for the government of the day to represent that the write-off it is asking the Canadian public to digest is simply a write-off of previous years' losses, or depreciations which should have been declared in earlier years. Also it is nice of the government to indicate, if that is cleared away, that somehow the CN will do better. When it is indicated that the depreciation should have been written off in previous years, the other side of it is that the government, in tolerating that lack of proper accounting, deliberately distorted the balance sheets of the CN in order to show a better picture over those years. That is the truth. The government tolerated an accounting principle which allowed CN to look somewhat better than otherwise, because it did not want to accept the complication of the adverse deficit position which the CN would show if proper accounting had been applied. That is a classic public service move. It is classic in the sense that it helps for the political future to disguise the facts. If that had been done in the private sector, it would have been damned from on high by the government of the day.
For political expediency, the government chose to distort and falsify, from an accounting standpoint, the statements in order to make them look better; accumulate what we are now being asked to write off, and who knows the difference? Unfortunately one can play with figures and his accounting approaches, but someone has to end up paying. If it was the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I would not feel so badly. Unfortunately it is not. He pays very little in taxes. The people who pay for the sheer, reckless, irresponsible mismanagement of this government are Canadian taxpayers. It is you, Mr. Speaker, I, and millions of others. Now we are being asked to agree to a new patchover in the case of CN.
Having spoken about that, I think no one should join in a debate touching upon the CN and the entire question of transportation without dealing generally with the whole question of the lack of proper commuter urban transit facilities in Canada. That brings me to what was one of the most colossal misrepresentations that any prime minister has ever come out with in the history of Canada. Of course, I am referring to the fact that our Prime Minister, in the midst of the 1974 election
March 3, 1978

campaign, solemnly vowed to inaugurate a $290 million program to aid urban transit in Canada.
Many who at that time still trusted the Prime Minister accepted his word. I can only assume that some even voted for him because he had spoken so forcefully about assisting urban transit in this country. That trust has been breached. In Toronto on June 17, 1974 the Prime Minister said:
-the federal government will pay 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles manufactured in Canada and 50 per cent of the cost of new stations and platforms forming part of the system . . .
He also promised "a Liberal program which would pay 25 per cent of the capital costs of all vehicles purchased for public transit". Those were the promises and many people put their trust in what was being said. The Prime Minister assured us that these promises were not pie in the sky. However, we soon realized that the immediate past minister of finance, the former member for Rosedale of all places, knew different. He told a Toronto press club conference that the government, after having spent more than $110 million to date on the stillborn Pickering airport development, and after spending another $400 million on air transport related industries, has no money left to carry out its election promises that had been so solemnly given by the Prime Minister of this country.
To me this is a clear example of the mistaken priorities of this government, and this augurs poorly for the tens of thousands who commute in the Toronto area each day. In my own area alone nearly every major urban transit project is now in jeopardy following the broken promise of this Prime Minister and his little servant, the Minister of Transport.
1 recite these things because I think the day has come in Canada when politicians must realize that such broken promises are unacceptable to the Canadian public and will no longer be tolerated. In my area in particular there has been great concern in respect of the activities of our rail transit facilities and the activities of the CNR, particularly in view of these broken promises of the Prime Minister.
I have received in the form of petitions and letters over 600 requests from constituents asking me to urge the government to reconsider its priorities and to honour its vital commitments to assist commuter interests in the Toronto area as well as in the York region and Simcoe county. I have the addresses and the names of these people who have written me recorded in the 600 petition forms, all available for delivery to Mr. Speaker on Monday. In short, we have 600 concerned Canadian voters who have indicated complete disdain for the broken promises of our Prime Minister and who intend to press their request for better commuter service in the Toronto area with all the means at their disposal. Let there be no doubt; between now and the next election, whenever it occurs, I intend to write each of those constituents bringing them up to date on the activities of this government with regard to commuter travel in the Toronto area.
Let me deal with another specific. The CNR, as most of us know, has a main line that runs from Toronto up through
Railway Act
Maple, King City, Aurora, Newmarket, Bradford, Lefroy, Stroud and Barrie. This was one of the earliest established rail lines in what was then known as Upper Canada. At one time it was a busy passenger route for people going to and from Toronto. This line was used at one time by many passengers who lived in the area and worked somewhere in Toronto or immediately north of the city. Then through lack of foresight on the part of this government and the inefficient operation of the CNR, we found that systematically that passenger service was phased out of operation. Systematically the passenger services on that line were downgraded so that eventually there was no railway at all. The hard fact is that as a result of the dissatisfaction the people who live in that area and their rather vehement, if you like, demands, we did get the promise of a commuter train. When did we get it? We got it on the eve of the 1972 election.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) who then represented the riding of York-Simcoe, in an eleventh hour repentance, somehow got someone at the government level to state the CNR would run a trial run on the line I have referred to, beginning a few days after the election on October 30, 1972. It was very fortunate that the constituents of York-Simcoe were discerning enough to realize that this was nothing more than a ploy; that it was just a base, disreputable, political ploy on the part of the government of the day to help the sitting member who was having difficulty being re-elected in that riding. The fact was that the government did not get re-elected with the majority it anticipated and the sitting member was defeated. That is why I am here. They did start a trial run and found it was amazingly successful. The government then tried to kill it, but having a minority government it did not have the guts to do so in face of the protest of those who still lived in the constituency.
The reason I refer to this is that we are now hearing ugly rumours from the bowels of this decrepit government, that somehow it thinks it may now be politically acceptable to kill that commuter train which has been running from Toronto up to Barrie. What I want from this Minister of Transport before this bill is passed is an unqualified commitment that the government will reverse its plans to end that commuter service which now runs between Toronto and Barrie. There is no reason to discontinue that line. We know it is marginally profitable-even those at CN will tell you that privately-and the figures speak for themselves.
Nevertheless this line has been carrying ever increasing numbers of commuters to and from Toronto. For example, in 1976 the total number of passengers who rode that train was 128,884. In 1977 the number was 146,037, or a percentage increase of 13.3 per cent. Most significantly, we find that in January 1977 there were a total of 309 who travelled south on the train and 301 who came back on an average each day during the month. Those are daily figures. In January, 1978, the figures down to Toronto were 388 and up from Toronto 379, in each case an increase of over 25 per cent. What those figures show is that the commuter line is becoming more and more popular with rising energy costs. With the congestion on

March 3, 1978
Railway Act
roads leading to Toronto, more and more people are starting to use the train service. 1 think this is not the time for the government to be considering the termination of that service, as has been rumoured.
What is unbelievable is that while the government quibbles about running that line, they have absolutely no quibble about the foolish idea of trying to establish a second airport at Toronto, namely, the aborted Pickering development which still lies in disarray to the east of my riding. Think, Mr. Speaker, of the money that they poured into that development, the good farm land that they destroyed by forcing out various farmers. Some $10 million has been devoted to purchasing land alone. The reason I emphasize this is that clearly we have a government whose priorities are completely out of whack.
Twenty years ago perhaps it made sense for them to be concentrating on aircraft and airport type development; but today technology has changed, people's thinking has changed and energy is becoming much more costly. We are in an era when commuter train travel should be particularly encouraged, not discouraged. The day has come when this government must be convinced to stop pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into white elephants such as Mirabel and other airport developments when those people who are going to and from work on a daily basis need better facilities to get them to and from work. That is the hard issue, and it is time that this cold, politically oriented government realized the facts. We do not need a Pickering airport in the Toronto area, we need better commuter transit facilities, and if this government will not give these to the Toronto area people, it is time that they were removed from power.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
1 say that because 1 think it is absolutely intolerable that we have a government which has refused to pay for the expenditure needed to realign the rail lines in the western part of the marshalling yards near Union station in Toronto. They have refused to put up the $50 million that is needed to realign those rail lines, which of course is their responsibility, and as a result of that refusal they have frustrated the GO train development throughout the northwest and western part of Toronto.
I notice the presence here of the hon. member from Mississauga, the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Abbott). If he were honest, he would take part in this debate and say there is considerable concern in his area, in his riding, regarding the inadequate commuter facilities to and from the western part of the Toronto area. Let there be no doubt that the reason for the lack of facilities-the Ontario government is willing to provide them and it has reserved the cash to pay for them-is that the federal government refuses to spend approximately $50 million for the realignment and development of the lines. Those are the facts. At the same time, the federal government is tolerating a loss on the virtually stillborn Mirabel airport project of over $50 million a year.

It is time that priorities were straightened out. Surely those who wish to get to and from work should be given a relatively high priority. At a time when we are trying to save energy and we are asking people to use smaller cars, we must enable them to use the railways and the rail cars which are available to get to and from work as opposed to frustrating them and even resisting the development of that type of commuter transit.
If hon. members read the history of CNR they will find that it is a classic example of a Crown corporation being said to be giving great service but in fact steadily downgrading the most meaningful service of all, in this case passenger service for the use of those who need it on a daily basis to get to and from work.
I know our time is limited, Mr. Speaker, but 1 would like to go through some of the quotations we have heard in the past of others speaking on behalf of the CNR who have said to the government: "If you will just relieve us of the debt we have run up, we will be better boys in the future. If we can somehow or other get away from the debt load, we will become profitable in the future".
Surely members of the House have every reason to start suspecting such statements. If there was any evidence-and I hope if the minister has it he can give it to the committee- which would show that if we can go along with this refinancing or recapitalization of CN, they will provide better commuter transit service in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Edmonton or Calgary, I would say let us get this bill through with virtually no debate-because we are doing something that the Canadian public need badly. What 1 am nervous about is that we will be asked to give another carte blanche and, if this bill goes through, allow them to sweep under the carpet the mistakes of previous years. Then when they have a nice clean book to work on they will be up to their old tricks of cutting down service, increasing their costs, and sticking the Canadian people with a never ending increase in their deficits.
Those are the facts. If this government was serious in trying to orient the CN to a more businesslike approach, why will they not let the private sector buy into the CN? Why will they not make available at least a portion of the CN stock to the private sector? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, why they will not do that. It is because Michael Pitfield, who sits at the right hand of the Prime Minister, says he does not like the idea; he does not think the private investor in this country should have a piece of any Crown corporation. His voice is much louder with the Prime Minister than that of our poor Minister of Transport. The fact is that we are being run not by a Cabinet but by an elite sitting around the emperor's quarters upstairs, and they have much more influence with the emperor, our Prime Minister, than any paltry minister, including the Minister of Transport.
In committee I hope to explore some of these items a little more fully and to have some questions answered with respect to the operation of CN. Also I would like clearer explanations why this depreciation item was run up in the first place and, secondly, why the CN thinks it can now be virtually dissolved simply by the rather convenient recapitalization to which they
March 3, 1978

refer. But, above all, I want to get some hard evidence of what they intend to do for commuter travellers in our major Canadian centres, including the Toronto area.
I think it is time the government was called to task for, first of all, making the promises which the Prime Minister made in the 1974 campaign, and, secondly, for so ruthlessly ignoring those promises, knowing the plight of the many commuters in the Toronto area.
With regard to this plight, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to extend an invitation to the Minister of Transport. If the minister is willing, I will ride with him on a commuter train into Toronto during the rush hour. I will watch him being jostled into a car. I will watch him standing for 20 to 30 minutes in a hot, crowded car going into Toronto in the morning and back at night, and I will see if he still has that little grin on his face which is like that of a Cheshire cat. The minister knows exactly the problems Torontonians are living with.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lang) were jostling back and forth. The hon. member said he would like the minister to be jostled on a commuter train. I am sure my colleagues from Newfoundland join me in wishing we had a train in which to be jostled.
I am pleased to have a few minutes to discuss Bill C-17 and the refinancing of the CNR. 1 can relate to some of the remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith). In many ways the northern part of Canada has the same problem we have in northern Newfoundland.
I would like to refer to something which was said by a former minister of transport, Senator Marchand. On March 17, 1974 he noted that transportation policy in Canada was based on the principle of competition. He stated that this principle was in part wrong for Canada because, if we looked at the size of the country and the distribution of its population,
Railway Act
we could see that we cannot have a transportation network which is economic everywhere. For example, we cannot have an economic system of transport in the north or in those regions of the country which are thinly populated. We cannot have an economic system in regions which are remote from the centre. The former minister went on to say that the principle of competition can apply where there is competition, but it will not work in places where there is no competition.
Over the years my colleagues have made the plea in this House for a good transportation policy in Newfoundland. In a submission presented by a union to the Sullivan commission we find the following words:
Transportation as is the case in all other regions of Canada is fundamental to that particular region's economic, social and cultural development. Railway systems in particular have shaped Canada.
I think the same thing applied when at the time of Confederation it was agreed that a great railway would span Canada from west to east in order to develop all parts of Canada and to take advantage of our resources. Section 31 of the terms of union back in 1949 stated the following:
At the date of Union, or as soon thereafter as practicable, Canada will take over the following services and will as from that date of Union relieve the Province of Newfoundland of the public costs incurred in respect of each service taken over, namely,
(a) the Newfoundland Railway, including steamship and other marine services;
Section 32 (1) states:
Canada will maintain in accordance with the traffic offering a freight and passenger steamship service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, which on completion of a motor highway between Corner Brook and Port aux Basques, will include suitable provision for the carriage of motor vehicles.
Much history has taken place. Many studies and commissions have been carried out with regard to the transportation system in Newfoundland and in Canada. If we were to recycle all the paper used by those commissions and studies we would probably drive the paper mills out of business.
There are only a couple of points I want to make. The minister knows there is a need to upgrade the Trans-Canada Highway, if it can be called that, in the province of Newfoundland. Anyone who has driven over the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland knows it has deteriorated. The minister knows it needs upgrading. I do not criticize the minister when he indicates that for this purpose we are going to get only $25 million, but 1 do not think that is enough. I realize it is the responsibility of the province to put up the remainder, but we will never do it. I appreciate the fact that $30 million to $50 million has been spent on a highway to the Great Northern Peninsula so that advantage can be taken of the natural resources there, but that highway must be coincidental with the Trans-Canada Highway from Port aux Basques to Deer Lake, which starts in the Great Northern Peninsula.
I hope the minister and his colleagues in cabinet will recognize that if we want to take advantage of the natural resources we have and if we want to contribute to Canada as a whole, we must have an economic base, and part of that is a proper transportation system. There can be no justification for the

March 3, 1978
Railway Act
present condition of the Trans-Canada Highway on the island of Newfoundland.
Mainland Canada, God bless it, has a Trans-Canada Highway and a rail system built to a higher level of performance than those in Newfoundland. We cannot accept a lower standard for the Trans-Canada Highway or for the rail system on the island of Newfoundland. The Trans-Canada Highway must be brought up to a standard which will permit the safe and efficient movement of private automobiles, trucks and buses for passenger movement. We need a standard to meet the requirement for the short and medium term for the movement of passengers.
The present road cruiser service does not come close to providing a satisfactory passenger service. I am sure that the only part of the Trans-Canada Highway in all Canada which is below standard is found in the province of Newfoundland. 1 think it can be said without any fear of doubt that the CNR, which is responsible for maintaining rail freight and express service, has now abandoned that service and is moving toward using rubber traffic. The increase in the use of rubber traffic in Newfoundland on the Trans-Canada Highway has increased by 424 per cent. The number of trucks using the highway has increased from 200 or 300 to 2,800 in just the last five years. I hope the minister recognizes that and that to contribute to Canadian society and the Canadian economy we must build up the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland.
Another problem which has arisen in my district concerns the coastal service. The city of Corner Brook has been the port and distribution point for goods and services going to the Great Northern Peninsula, the northern part of Newfoundland, and Labrador further north. Through some agreement made in 1968 or 1969, this service was to be abandoned in favour of a service between Blanc-Sablon in Labrador and St. Barbe. The subsidy provided is adequate and will give a much needed service across the Strait of Belle Isle, but we should not trade off that service for the greater service from Corner Brook up the Great Northern Peninsula and to Labrador. Now the wholesalers and sellers of goods and services in that area will have to use the Trans-Canada Highway to transport goods to Lewisporte and then transship them down the coast, which is more costly and inefficient.
I understand there is a commitment to get second reading of Bill C-17 and Bill C-7 through, Mr. Speaker. I am willing to go along with that and postpone my further remarks until report stage or third reading. 1 want to repeat that I hope the minister will consider very carefully these two vital needs of Newfoundland. The first is that there should be reconsideration of the amount of money necessary to upgrade and strenghten the Trans-Canada Highway for the future; and the second is that he consider the appeal to the water transportation commission from certain community leaders and businessmen about the coastal service from the west coast of Newfoundland which is so necessary to transport goods and services to northern Newfoundland and Labrador.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to support the excellent remarks of my colleague the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). Perhaps I could pick up where he left off.
I realize that the three maritime provinces have just signed an agreement with the federal government on a 50-50 cost sharing basis for the upgrading of the Trans-Canada Highway. If the minister were honest about this, I think a special case could be made for Newfoundland receiving greater federal participation in the upgrading of the Trans-Canada Highway. He knows as well as I that CN has been downgrading and withdrawing its rail services in Newfoundland since 1968 when it withdrew the rail passenger service, notwithstanding the provisions clearly set out in the terms of union. That is another argument, however.
It can be argued, and perhaps one day will be, that what the federal government is doing with respect to railways in Newfoundland is illegal and unconstitutional. But they are doing it. They are phasing out rail service in the province of Newfoundland, rail service which was given to them in trust by the people of Newfoundland in 1949 to operate for them as part of the agreement of the terms of union. We lost the railway passenger service and we are losing the freight service. They have allowed the roadbed to deteriorate to the point that it is not economic to upgrade it.
The consequence of that is that more and more traffic is being diverted to the Trans-Canada Highway. More and more freight is being hauled across the province on the Trans-Canada Highway by CN trucks. This is causing rapid deterioration of the highway because it is being used to an extent that was never planned. It was never designed to carry that amount of freight.
It was an inadequate road at best because it was hastily built. We are grateful that it was built, of course, because it was the first road across the province, but it is in desperate need of upgrading. It pays the CN to divert traffic from the rail service to the Trans-Canada Highway because they do not have to pay a cent toward maintaining that highway, whereas they have to bear the total responsibility and cost of maintaining the rail roadbed.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I think a case can be made for greater federal participation in the agreement to upgrade the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland. The province has held out for a 75-25 sharing agreement and I think this can be more than justified. We do not expect, certainly under this administration, to see any move toward upgrading the roadbed by making the necessary repairs, eliminating the curves and making it an efficient rail line. It has become an expensive proposition as a result of almost ten years of neglect and deterioration. The federal government should recognize it assumed an obligation by allowing CN to downgrade its rail service, both passenger and freight; by diverting freight to the Trans-Canada Highway it has assumed a responsibility toward the cost of maintaining that road.

March 3, 1978

My colleague has described the condition of the road. There are places in the province now where the road is virtually impassable. The province is on the verge of imposing strict load limits because the deterioration is so bad. We do not know what to expect this next spring but we can expect the road will be seriously undermined to the point that it may be necessary to halt traffic altogether in order to make necessary repairs.
That brings me to the next point, Mr. Speaker, the withdrawal of another essential service, CN marine. I see my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in the House. He has written about this, and so have I. Contrary to the spirit if not to the terms of union, we see in Newfoundland a withdrawal of the administrative branch of the CN marine service from Newfoundland to either Moncton or Halifax. The minister can deny this if he will but the facts speak for themselves.
Notwithstanding the fact that a royal commission was appointed by this government to examine all phases of CN operations in Newfoundland and the undertaking given at the time of setting up that royal commission-that no substantial decisions would be made affecting the service until the commission had completed its hearings, today the CN is withdrawing the administrative branch of its marine service to the mainland. When about 78 per cent of CN marine operations, either the coastal service or the ferry service, arc in Newfoundland, it makes no sense to have the administration in Moncton which is not even a seaport.

speakeroldname: Mr. Eldon M. Woolliams (Calgary North) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-227, to amend the Criminal Code (invasion of privacy), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for permitting this bill to come up at this time because it is very timely. Bill C-227 is a private member's bill to amend the Criminal Code in reference to the invasion of privacy. I will divide my argument into two parts. I will deal with the contents of this bill. However, before 1 do so I want to say this bill has to do with one of the most important questions in reference to civil rights before the Canadian people today.
1 want to read from a book by John M. Carroll entitled "The Third Listener". When I refer to privacy 1 am talking about wiretapping, bugging or any other kind of form of electronic surveillance. This is what the writer says in his book which was written 10 years ago, and the situation is far worse today:
Even when there's no great hurry, getting a court order is a bother, involving a showing of probable cause to believe that the wiretap or bug will produce information about a crime. And, although law enforcers will argue this point by the hour, the fact is that very few taps or bugs produce firm evidence or hot leads. For police officers to go to court time after time for wiretap permission and then never turn up any valuable wiretap permission is embarrassing after a while. It's far easier for them to pool their own money and buy their own private equipment, tap one suspicious phone after another without an order till they find a live one, then get the court order-
With a device the size of the emblem on my ring today one can wiretap at 200 feet or more an hour's conversation between parties, it is therefore with great pride that I move this bill today having to do with a very serious amendment to the Criminal Code.
In 1972 when we had a minority government it was men like Ron Atkey from the Toronto, St. Paul's riding, Gordon Fair-weather, myself and others who pressed amendments to the Criminal Code with reference to privacy of the individual in Canada. Following that, as soon as this government gained a majority they repealed those sections and took away what 1 say has eroded the civil rights of people in this nation.
What does this bill do? It amends sections dealing with the question of electronic surveillance, wiretapping and bugging. It proposes six or seven factors. It outlaws all authorizations, all wiretapping and all types of electronic surveillance in reference to solicitors' telephone consultations with their clients.
1 hear it said over and over again that if you have nothing to hide, what have you to worry about from a wiretap?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext:
That's right.

March 3, 1978

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member says that's right. I am sorry to hear him say that because the whole idea of confidentiality between solicitor and client is eroded. There are many cases in which this type of electronic surveillance has taken place. I will be quoting later in my address this afternoon very important lawyers, Queen's counsel in Toronto, the Advocacy Society of Ontario, Mr. Chapel and Mr. Cooper.
The whole of the law in reference to electronic surveillance as it pertains to voluntary statements made by any person regarding charges laid, alleged or proposed, goes out the window. In fact, telephones are no longer your friend in Canada, they are your fink. These important trial lawyers say that if you are going to interview your clients, it is safer to go into the park in Toronto or drive out to a farm field in the country. Because no longer can you do business over the telephone, one of the most important instruments for a lawyer and his client.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Let's be serious for a moment. This is a very serious subject. I do not mind being interrupted, but not with nonsense. Under the Canadian Bill of Rights and under the common law of this country, every person in Canada is entitled to a solicitor, even the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt). I want to thank the Chair for agreeing to extra time.
I pay a great compliment to the Chair for granting extra time on so important a subject.
This bill would also prevent the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) from issuing warrants authorizing wiretaps and, therefore, interceptions by way of warrants against candidates after the writ is issued calling for a federal election. Why do I emphasize that? Under the Protection of Privacy Act, the Official Secrets Act was amended.
The Solicitor General may issue a warrant authorizing the interception or issue of any communication if he is satisfied by the evidence or on oath that such and such may be true. But under what conditions? We are all candidates for one party of another. The act refers to "activities directed toward accomplishing governmental change within Canada''. Good gracious I have been in eight elections, in two of which I advocated a change and we got it. Since then the Liberal party has been in power. Are we going to have a law in Canada that permits the Solicitor General to wiretap candidates' telephones because they advocate a change in government? I say to my friends across the way, what may work for them on one occasion will work against them on another. 1 say in this bill that we must have an amendment to protect political candidates seeking public office so that conversations between them and their supporters or those who may oppose them will be kept confidential. Surely that is the very art of electioneering.
Let me refer to section 6(2) of the Protection of Privacy Act as it pertains to the Official Secrets Act, and also section 6(3) of the Protection of Privacy Act as it pertains to the Official Secrets Act, which refers to activities directed toward accomplishing governmental change within Canada or elsewhere. Of late we have seen three solicitors general come and go. Words
Criminal Code
they utter on Wednesday, speaking metaphorically, with reference to electronic surveillance and wiretapping contradict information on Friday coming from people giving evidence under oath before commissions and from other sources.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated the RCMP would not have been able to conduct a proper investigation and obtain proper evidence and information with reference to Japanese terrorists if it had not been for opening mail. We have seen solicitors general come and go as quickly as 1 change my clothes. We have heard them say that members of parliament were not wiretapped, yet we find that even the former solicitor general was wiretapped. Electronic surveillance was used against him, and the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) and we do not know how many others. As the book "The Third Listener" states, we will never know unless it comes out through a witness or a commission. You cannot pry the facts out of the government. Having seen three solicitors general come and go, I would say with that record, beware.
Fourth, this bill declares that all interceptions made illegally that is, by the bugging of telephones-which produce evidence of any kind will be inadmissible as evidence in any court of law against any person unless such interceptions are the result of legal authorization granted by a judge. The reason for raising this question is that the Supreme Court of Canada has set out that the following is the law. In their Lordships' opinion, the test to be applied in considering whether evidence is admissible is whether it is relevant to the matters in issue. If it is relevant, it is admissible and the court is not concerned with how the evidence was obtained.
That is the judgment of the highest court of our land, outside of parliament. In other words, the Supreme Court of Canada has ruled that even if evidence is obtained surreptitiously, by plots, illegal wiretaps or the beating of prisoners, if it is relevant to the issue, it goes in. That is against all the fundamental rules governing jurisprudence and the common law that we have in Canada and, indeed, in the United Kingdom.
I repeat, the Supreme Court of Canada rule as the law stands today is that, even if the evidence is obtained surreptitiously, if it is relevant to the issue it is admissible as evidence. The court has stated that it does not matter how the evidence is obtained. I see some good lawyers across the way. We have a very good Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Some members of that committee are not lawyers, but it is a good committee. 1 do not think that any Canadian is prepared to accept that kind of law. On the other hand, many Canadians do not think about this unless they, or their son or daughter, are in trouble.
A few years ago 1 defended people getting three or four years for simple possession of marijuana. I was criticized in my constituency for doing that; I received a letter of criticism. Not long after, the very man who wrote to me said that his son had gotten in trouble as a result of a soft drug, marijuana, and was sentenced. The shoe was then on the other foot.
Time and again the courts have said that if the law goes too far, if we usurp the civil rights of the individual, it is up to

March 3, 1978
Criminal Code
parliament to correct the law. That is what I am recommending today, that parliament correct the law. It is not for the courts to interpret the law the way they wish it to be. When the law is weak, you do not require the order which the law calls for because you can get the evidence in through the back door. As the writer of this book says, you can buy wiretap equipment as small as the insignia on my ring. Then once you find something, you rush to the courthouse to get an order. Even worse, you do not need to obtain an order but can apply to get the evidence in. If it is relevant to the issue, in it goes. I think it is high time we changed that kind of law, which was brought in by people who maintain, as they have with respect to other matters, that they are the great foundation of the Civil Liberties Association.
Further, all evidence obtained as a result of the use of an electronic device, whether lawfully or unlawfully, must be destroyed within two years of the trial and appeals being completed. In other words, after the due process of law has been carried out, evidence obtained as a result of electronic surveillance must be destroyed.
We are building up in this era of technical know-how information banks, which mean that the whole privacy of individuals has been eroded. We shall soon be able to press a button and find out how many times people go to the washroon or how many times they have gone. The time has come to take a look at the law of privacy. I am not only seeking the support of members of my party but of members generally. I see some here today who have spoken out in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs; 1 shall not name them because I do not want to leave any impression that I am criticizing people because they have different ideas. If we all think alike, there is no thinking.
I never could accept that if the Tories or Liberals happened to disagree among themselves on some issue there was something sinister about it. I do not always agree with my party and I do not expect the party will always agree with me. I think that is healthy. I am not a trained seal. This amendment is designed to protect a person who has been subject to interception, and anyone violating this rule would be subject to prosecution for an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for two years. I think we have to put some teeth into this thing.
The bill also restores to the Criminal Code the 90-day notice requirement. Notice must be given to any person who has been the object of electronic surveillance. Nevertheless, a judge is permitted to extend the 90-day period if evidence is produced that longer time is needed to look into offences such as syndicated crimes and conspiracies, especially in the field of drugs. I go along with that, but 1 say that in ordinary cases everyone who is the object of electronic surveillance should be notified after the event. And I go further. 1 say that if there is no legal authorization, then evidence should not be used; neither should evidence obtained as a result of listening in be used. In the absence of such protection, every day an ounce of

freedom goes. There are only so many onces of freedom in this nation, freedom which is being eroded every day. We saw an instance this week in what took place with reference to the hon. member for Leeds.

speechtext:
Lord Sankey said in the Woolmington case in 1935:
Throughout the web of the English Criminal law, one golden thread is always to be seen, that it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt. . . the principle that the prosecution must prove the guilt of the prisoner is part of the common law of England and no attempt to whittle it down can be entertained.
This principle has been asserted time and time again by the courts of Canada. Therefore, any evidence which is obtained by plots, plans or lies, or secured surreptitiously, should not be admitted. The intention underlying this rule is to ensure that the evidence is true.
Let me remind the hon. member who interrupted me that I have served as counsel during many serious cases and I have found, through interrogation of officers, that sometimes confessions have been obtained which were subsequently shown to be untrue. Suspects had confessed rather than put up with interrogation. 1 have not time to give many examples, but here is one. A Canadian was being beat up in jail in Chicago and he confessed to the Henderson murder which had taken place five years earlier in Calgary and which was still unsolved. What happened? When the police checked the story they found the statement was not true.

speechtext:
I shall try to be brief, Mr. Speaker. I just want to make one more point to show the House how this matter has got out of hand. I want to quote from Hansard of March 2, 1978, in which the hon. member for Leeds is reported as having said:
I must mention another thing. 1 do not like to do this, but 1 think it is necessary. In that document there was included a statement by Superintendent Bentham of the RCMP in which he summarized a conversation he had with me a few days ago. It is quite true that I had a conversation with him. His statement was accurate with the exception of one point. I think this is a very serious interfer-
March 3, 1978

ence with the privileges of Members of Parliament. 1 am paraphrasing again. Superintendent Bentham reported to the Solicitor General and his superiors that I asked him whether he was recording or bugging our conversation, and that he replied yes. I must tell the House that that is an absolute falsehood. I did ask him whether he was bugging or recording our conversation, and he replied "No". He said, "If you mean I am making notes of what you are saying, yes I am. Do you mind?" I said, "No, of course not."
Mr. Speaker, 1 have had police superintendents back down in similar circumstances under cross-examination. "Recording" is not "taking notes". That is no excuse for that misrepresentation. The report continues:
However, the report he handed to his superiors-which I saw with my own eyes because it was handed to me by the Solicitor General-said that Superintendent Bentham said that my telephone call and the words I was using were being recorded . . .
What manner of nonsense is that? Is it not time we had a law which says that that kind of misrepresentation, that kind of evidence, if it got into a courtroom, should be declared inadmissible? The hon. member for Leeds continued:
I questioned General Dare about this and he said it was just a matter of terminology. I think it is much more than just a matter of terminology. The main point I am trying to brin out is that I feel any Canadian has the right to legal advice.
He asked whether he was being recorded, and he was told he was not. Then he was told yes, by Dare. So the House can see what a frightening situation we are getting into. In fact, we are getting into a very unusual and poisonous climate in this country when these things can go on in reference to even a member of parliament and when we find they are almost condoned and accepted. If this matter should go beyond this great court, this parliament, I hope that any judge would declare such a statement inadmissible on the ground it had been obtained illegally. This was bugging-illegal bugging. No notice had been given, no authorization. There was a complete lie as to whether he was being bugged or not.
Therefore, with all the spirit I have and with all the intelligence at my command, I ask parliament to change the kind of law which is whittling away the privacy of Canadians every day. If the law is not serving the public, no one will have respect for it-and no one will obey it. The law is an ass.

Criminal Code
of terrorists. What would the hon. member do in that instance? How would he handle it?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would require proof that these lawyers or solicitors are part of the Mafia. Even the Mafia is entitled to a fair trial and counsel. Everyone is. If the hon. member has any information which indicates that a lawyer is a member of the Mafia and is breaking the law, he should report it to the Law Society of the area in which the lawyer is practicing, whether it be Quebec, Ontario, Alberta or British Columbia. That question is very easy to answer.
Regarding consultation between lawyers and clients, there must be confidentiality. Lawyers cannot operate any other way. That is a fundamental rule. It did not come in just because of someone's whim. It has been the rule for 400 years under the British system of jurisprudence.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate because I am interested in the matter, as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) realized during the sittings of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs last year. That committee was studying the Criminal Code amendments suggested by the government to clear up the Criminal Code provisions governing the protection of privacy and the use of wiretapping when its use is deemed to be necessary.
In any event in spite of my comments on his bill, I am convinced that the hon. member for Calgary North will not think that I am ill-intentioned. Indeed he is well aware of my own concern about those extraordinary investigation procedures when used indiscriminately. He remembers the very specific questions I had then put to the Minister of Justice concerning the use of those extraordinary investigation procedures and safeguards available to individuals involved once those means must be used.
Mr. Speaker, first we must understand why the government of Canada has considered it necessary to include in the Criminal Code provisions specifying circumstances and conditions when wiretapping or electronic surveillance may be used to fight the criminal elements of our society and particularly organized crime. Let us not forget that some years ago, there was no such provision in the Criminal Code. With the development of technology and particularly the increasingly elaborate devices at the disposal of criminal elements and particularly organized crime, it was essential that the government be able to fight the systematic erosion of our society by criminal elements through the use of similar devices just as elaborate, 1 admit, but necessary to help Canadian police forces to bring those criminals to court so that they be judged and sentenced to ensure a better protection of our society. This is the background of the inclusion of these provisions in the Criminal Code. Yet, after four years of implementation, we realized that criminals became more and more sophisticated in their

March 3, 1978
Criminal Code
attacks against our society and that the existing provisions of the Criminal Code no longer allowed our police forces to fight organized crime efficiently because of the extremely severe restrictions included in the legislation to protect the civil liberties of Canadians.
In all that wiretapping issue, Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely essential that we try to balance as much as possible the protection of civil liberties and the possibility of giving our police forces the investigation tools needed to bring those very well organized criminals before the courts and convict them. This is the issue, the balance between the protection of civil liberties and on the other hand the war, I said "war", against organized criminals who are infiltrating our society to destroy it.
Mr. Speaker, we shall remember that the then minister of justice suggested to expand the scope of the legislation on the invasion of privacy, commonly referred to as the wiretapping law, in order to give the police forces of our country adequate means to fight organized crime. At the time, as recorded in Hansard, I had voiced the most serious reservations about those new possibilities provided to the police. I had expressed the wish that at second reading stage the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs could examine that question in depth and try to strike that desirable balance between the two elements I just mentioned.
With leave, Mr. Speaker, I will limit myself to purely legal considerations. I somewhat deplore that when discussing a rather technical bill-and I know the hon. member for Calgary North has an obvious interest in that question, and I respect him all the more for that interest and the way he has in the past upheld his ideas in that area-he added at the end of his remarks some considerations that in my opinion have absolutely no bearing on the bill before us today, particularly when he referred to the problems we have had this week in the House when the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) raised a question of privilege, on which has not yet been decided upon.
So, except for this comment which I think shows that the question raised by the hon. member for Leeds has nothing to do with this bill, which is of an extremely technical nature, 1 shall proceed to simply explain the impact one of the clauses of Bill C-227 would have on our legal proceedings and also on the investigation methods available to our police forces.
Mr. Speaker, I refer to section 178(16) of the Criminal Code as worded now, and to the amendments proposed in clause 3 of Bill C-227 concerning this section 178(16). Section 178(16) clearly specifies the cases in which a judge can or cannot accept evidence obtained directly or indirectly by the bugging of a private communication. Mr, Speaker, the hon. member for Calgary North mentioned earlier the case law and the state of the law in common law as far as direct or indirect evidence obtained illegally is concerned. I respect him highly as a lawyer and a jurist and I wonder whether I misinterpreted his remarks, but he suggested that the present state of the law

in common Law is that, as a rule, evidence obtained directly or indirectly by an illegal bugging device could not be admitted evidence.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is the opposite and that in 1972, when we introduced these provisions in the Criminal Code ...

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext: Order, please. Would the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont allow the hon. member for Calgary North a question?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just like to rise on a point of order, without intending to delay. 1 know the hon. member would not want me to misquote him. I quoted directly from Mr. Justice Martland's judgment. I said that anything which is relevant to the issue is admissible. I was applying that to the common law. What I did say was that to have another law would be contrary to the principles of the common law that governed. 1 am not saying that under the common law the evidence is not admissible. There is the distinction.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INVASION OF PRIVACY PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for these details concerning his intervention. 1 think it was important because he had given the House a different impression from what he has just explained. But Mr. Speaker, if I may, 1 want to come back to the matter 1 was discussing. In 1972, the government deviated from Common Law tradition by not allowing in wiretapping cases the submission of evidence obtained directly or indirectly through illegal wiretaps, and that was not in compliance with the Common Law at that time.
In 1977, the government did want to realign wiretapping practices with the Common Law tradition and once again I expressed very serious reservations at that time. And in the course of the debate within the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which lasted several weeks, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) explained why according to the Department of Justice and law enforcement agencies, it was important to return to the traditional rules of Common Law concerning evidence resulting directly or indirectly from illegal wiretapping. And that evidence was not subjected to legal voir dire, so that any judge could accept or reject such evidence in order that justice be done.
The reasons were quite simple Mr. Speaker, because those so-called voir dire instances during which the judge had to listen to illegal tapes on which the disputed information was recorded, would determine whether submitting, not the tape itself-because it cannot be accepted according to our present law when it is illegally obtained-but indirect evidence, that evidence was not allowed, would prevent doing justice and that therefore he would authorize at that time by law allowing that evidence, if he thought that justice could not be done if he did
March 3, 1978

not accept it. Which caused absolutely unbelievable legal delays and slowed down the normal process of justice, and 1 am only quoting facts, I am not making a judgment on the point in question and the soundness or not of the allegations that were made at the time. In any case, that was the reason for wanting to come back to the common law as it existed. At the time I raised a point of great concern to me, namely that from the time a judge must admit as evidence evidence obtained directly or indirectly from an illegal wiretap, the wiretap itself becomes irrelevant in the trial if the Crown decides not to introduce it as evidence. Consequently this opened the door to extremely dangerous police abuses, potential abuses, I admit, but still abuses. And here 1 agree with the hon. member for Calgary North that it is extremely important to protect our society against potential abuses, abuses that I do not fear in the present context of our society but, once again, the law is often there for difficult cases, crisis situations, and who knows when a crisis situation occurs if we can really rely on the established institutions.
Well, I had said, Mr. Speaker, this matter of the relevance of the tap itself was the crucial point of that whole issue because, on the one hand, once again, we want criminals to be sentenced. We do not want a relevant piece of evidence to be ruled inadmissible in a trial on the pretence that it was obtained from an illegal tap or any other means not provided for in the law and consequently for criminals to be able to get away with it and justice not being done. That is not what we want. We want to protect civil liberties and know how to protect them and be quite certain that if that evidence is accepted and a criminal is convicted on the introduction of that evidence, that on the other hand the person who acted illegally in the exercise of his duties, the policeman, the RCMP or anyone else, will not be able to get away with it since in any case as a result the introduction-and here I come to the basic point-of a small provision-it is quite small but it is fundamental-under section 178 (16) of the Criminal Code as it now stands, an amendment that was introduced by the minister before the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs at my instigation, an amendment which reads as follows, and I quote:
Notwithstanding subsection (1) (which provides for the cases of admissibility), the judge or magistrate presiding at any proceedings may refuse to admit evidence obtained directly or indirectly as a result of information acquired by interception of a private communication that is itself inadmissible as evidence where he is of the opinion that the admission thereof would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
Here are four words which are absolutely fundamental to this debate. Why? Because they enable the court to call prosecution witnesses to the stand and to ask them: How did you obtain your evidence? Surveillance becomes relevant to the trial and I am convinced-and this may not be the opinion of other members-that we have inluded in the Criminal Code sufficient protection to prevent police forces or unscrupulous individuals from misusing the law and tainting our whole legal
Criminal Code
system. I know that this provision has not yet been tested before the Supreme Court and I am impatient for this to happen. For the moment however, what the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) seems to want is the guarantee that henceforth the institutions no longer be free to commit inadmissible abuses. If this is what he wants, Mr. Speaker, and I also want it, I believe the provision in section 178 (16), as it now stands in our Criminal Code, is sufficient assurance on this, because at the trial stage evidence that is illegal in itself remains pertinent. Therefore the judge, although he must allow indirect evidence, will be in a position to ask the Crown: Where did you get that evidence? So he can find out whether it has been obtained illegally or not. And through this, the policemen or other law-breaking person that will have willingly abused the law to tarnish our image of justice can be charged at a later hearing, so that improprer practices may be denounced.
Were it not for that provision, Mr. Speaker, 1 would be in total agreement with the hon. member for Calgary North. He will not doubt remember that at that time, 1 cross-examined the minister for more than two months on the implications of the original proposals that would have allowed a judge to accept either direct or indirect evidence from illegal wiretapping. He could never satisfy me on the issue of the pertinence of wiretapping as such, and this is why this provision was finally introduced to meet my own objections and concerns.
Mr. Speaker, I would conclude on this. There are many other things in the bill. It is an interesting legislation, because it deals with two things of concern to Canadians, namely the protection of basic freedoms and the fight against organized crime. I commend him for discussing this today, but I feel that the concerns be voiced while commenting on the bill do not justify the suggestion that the door is now open for police forces to do as they please. Because judicial protection remains, and I myself as a member of this House am confident that our courts can enforce the law while protecting our basic liberties.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this bill because, as my colleague the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) said, it is a serious question. I also welcomed the contribution, as I always do, of the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance). 1 do not always agree with him-I do not think that is always important-but I think the thoughtfulness behind his remarks is a good indication of how important it is that this be a subject matter which continues to be examined most appropriately in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Before I get to that, I want to make a remark on the intervention of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) because he put a very important question and I want to

enlarge on it, if I may. I do not remember his exact words, but 1 think he referred to solicitors or barristers who may be acting hand in hand with the Mafia. I think we are on dangerous ground when we talk about that. I am sure my colleague would know that there are barristers of great integrity and ability who might attract a series of clients of this nature. But 1 dare say he is not accusing that type of barrister of being part of the Mafia operation, and that was not what 1 took from his remarks. I would point out to him that it is darned hard to tell the difference sometimes.
I do not think the parallel would be a good one, but I will relate to the hon. member what happened to me when 1 was a very new barrister. I had the fortune-I am not sure whether the ill fortune or the good fortune-of securing an acquittal on a sex perversion charge. The next 15 months 1 had every sexual assault, indecent assault, incest and rape case in my county, until some other young solicitor managed to secure an acquittal on a similar charge and, thank heavens, they all went to him. Perhaps the comparison is not a remarkably good one, but I would hate to think that because I attracted all these cases, I was acting hand in hand with that type of criminal.
Let me come to what I believe is the importance of this bill. I believe in its substance but, more important, I believe it is a vehicle in which the matter can become the subject matter of discussion in the appropriate forum, namely the standing committee.
Much has been said about how well and diligently that committee has operated. 1 will not repeat that because it is almost trite now, and anyway, that is the way a committee should operate. 1 do not think we have to brag about that, and I hope it will continue. But 1 want the bill before the committee for one very important reason-at least to me it is important-and it is very seldom that 1 use the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as the basis for my argument. Among other things, at his press conference yesterday he said he detected a cynicism, a skepticism or suspicion-I cannot remember the exact words he used and I do not know in what context he put it. Well, I detect the same cynicism, skepticism or suspicion. I do not want to be overly partisan about it, but if we look at the national security side, at least one reason for that cynicism is that assurances which were given-perhaps with complete integrity, I do not know; perhaps in all good faith, I do not know-had to be withdrawn, changed or modified. I take no partisan satisfaction in saying that and 1 am sure 1 felt for the various solicitors general much the same as did my colleagues opposite. It is a very serious thing when you are giving assurances to the House and the Canadian people about a
matter of national security and then several days later you have to withdraw them.
With respect to this type of legislation, obviously it can lead to suspicion and cynicism. On the side of the Official Secrets Act, the reporting is very limited. We have all received the report days or weeks ago and we know it is one page long because those are the provisions. One may say, and I might agree, that you cannot have a full report on national security matters because it would not be secret; but I say that we have no assurance whatsoever-as a matter of fact, we have evidence to the contrary-on such matters as wiretapping or the Official Secrets Act, that even the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) knows of evidence to the contrary. No wonder people are suspicious.
On the criminal side, with respect to organized crime and such things, of course we have to fight sophisticated crime with sophisticated method. But there is a danger in thinking that a husband and wife taking bets in a cigar shop are part of organized crime. Only a vigilant, diligent study of the report that we receive annually will help. That report will have to be studied in committee. I am referring to the report required under the Criminal Code and the Protection of Privacy Act.
I commend this bill to the House as a good vehicle with which to put a serious and important matter before the proper forum, that forum being the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, in joining the debate on Bill C-227 1 wish to say that the hon. member who sponsored the bill has done a service by bringing it forward because it gives us another opportunity to debate this important matter.
In the very short time available to me, I want to look at the bill from the point of view of a layman rather than a practitioner of the art, so to speak. The reservations expressed by those who are solicitors with regard to the present statutes are understandable when you listen to their arguments, but 1 do not think the majority of the Canadian people who happen not to be lawyers are particularly impressed by these arguments. Obviously if a lawyer is in the business of defending people in a court of law, he will use every avenue open to him.
